title: Women who carried hadith
hookLine: Aisha, and later scholars like Karimah al-Marwaziyyah, who taught Bukhari's Sahih

cards: Cover me, cover me. A man has come home from a cave on a mountain, his heart pounding, and those are his words to his wife.
It's the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, home from Hira, at the beginning of revelation, and the report sits near the start of Sahih al-Bukhari. Who tells it? A woman: Aisha, his wife.
Inside her telling, another woman answers him. And much later, a third woman would sit with this very book and teach it. Today, women who carried hadith.

teach.b: First, Aisha, the narrator, whom you've met before as a scholar in her own right. She tells of the cave, the angel, the command to read, and the Prophet coming home shaken.

Her account of the beginning sits on the book's opening pages. She's also the source for reports on how he prayed at night, how he lived at home, what he said in private. Second, Khadijah, inside the story.
In Aisha's telling, the Prophet tells Khadijah he fears for himself.

teach.h: KHADIJAH: ALLAH WILL NEVER DISGRACE YOU.
teach.b: And Khadijah answers: never, by Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. Then she says why. You keep ties with your relatives.
You carry the burdens of the weak. You help the one who has nothing. You honor your guest.
You stand by people in their hardships. Then she takes him to her cousin Waraqah. So the first comfort in this report comes from a woman, and the report itself comes from a woman.

Third, Karimah, the teacher. Long after, a scholar named Karimah al-Marwaziyyah taught Bukhari's Sahih in Mecca. Students came to read the book with her, and wrote her into their chains: she narrated it to us.
Her name went into the line by which this book was handed on. Fourth, the shape of it. One book, three women.
A woman tells the story. Inside it, a woman gives the first comfort.
And a woman teaches the book that holds them both. The science this path has followed for weeks asks of every narrator: trustworthy? careful? did they really hear it?

teach.h: THE SAME QUESTIONS, THE SAME CHAINS.
teach.b: Women narrators were asked the same questions. Their names are in the chains because of the answers.

how: Students of hadith learn the names of women narrators and teachers, from Aisha onward, and some modern scholars have gathered their lives into studies of their own.

games.q: what does “women who carried hadith” mean?
o: women who wrote down the Qur'an during revelation
the wives of the Prophet, and no other women at all
women narrators and teachers, tested like everyone else

games.q: women who carried hadith — tap the pairs.

s: the report of how revelation began comes through Aisha
it sits on the first pages of al-Bukhari's Sahih, in her telling.
women narrators were held to easier standards
they were asked the same questions as everyone: trustworthy, careful, did they hear it?
in the report, Khadijah tells the Prophet to stay silent
she says Allah will never disgrace you, lists his good deeds, and takes him to Waraqah.

games.q: you're Khadijah. your husband comes home from the mountain trembling, afraid for himself. what do you say?
o: 'never, by Allah: Allah will never disgrace you,' and you name his good deeds.
games.why: she reassures him by naming what he does: keeps ties of kin, carries the weak, helps the one with nothing, honors guests. then she takes him to Waraqah.

practice: Three women, three parts: Aisha, who told it; Khadijah, who comforted; Karimah, who taught it. Choose one and keep her name.

Then go back to Khadijah's list, ties with relatives, the burdens of the weak, the one who has nothing, the guest, people in hardship, and notice which one someone has done for you, and which is within your reach; if you pray, you can remember these women in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Women who carried hadith. From Aisha, who narrated, to Karimah al-Marwaziyyah, who taught Bukhari's Sahih: women in the chains, tested like everyone else. Today's word.

orig.note: 'she narrated to us': how a chain names a woman who taught the report.

carryVoice: Your line: she taught the sahih. One book, three women. See you on the next page.
